title: Part X ITAA 1936 — CFC attribution rules
summary: Attribution of the income of controlled foreign companies (CFCs) to Australian residents. A company resident in a listed or unlisted country is a CFC if 5 or fewer Australian entities hold 50%+ control (or a single entity 40%+, or de facto control), provided it is not a Part X Australian resident (boundary carve-out). An attributable taxpayer (10%+ interest) is taxed on its attribution percentage of the CFC's attributable income. The active income test (tainted income ratio under 5%) is the central gate: CFCs that pass it are attributed only limited amounts; unlisted country CFCs that fail it have all income attributed, while listed country CFCs that fail it are attributed only concession-income tainted amounts. Attribution accounts then make distributions tax-free. Subsection coverage: operative ss 340, 349-350, 352, 356-357, 361-363, 382-393, 432-433, 446-448, 451, 456-457 mapped to nodes; ss 317, 318-331, 334-348, 351, 353-355, 358-360, 364-381, 389-391, 394-431, 434-445, 449-450, 452-455, 458-461A (machinery/definitions); ss 462-468 (records/transitional).

nodes.label: An Australian resident entity holds an interest in a foreign company (directly or through interposed entities)
nodes.body: Part X of the ITAA 1936 attributes income of a controlled foreign company (CFC) to Australian residents with a sufficient interest in it. If the CFC's income is attributed, you are taxed on your share of its attributable income — mainly its passive (tainted) income — even though it has not been distributed.

statute.title: Controlled foreign company (CFC)

nodes.label: The foreign company derives income or profits in a statutory accounting period
nodes.body: The attribution rules operate by statutory accounting period (normally the company's accounting year). If the company is a CFC with attributable income for the period, the income is attributed to attributable taxpayers in the year of income in which the period ends (s 456).

statute.title: Assessability in respect of CFC's attributable income

nodes.label: Is the company a resident of a listed country or an unlisted country?
nodes.body: The Part applies only to companies resident (for tax purposes) in a listed country — countries with broadly comparable tax systems set out in the regulations (e.g. Canada, France, Germany, Japan, UK, US, NZ) — or an unlisted country (everywhere else). A company is resident in a listed country if it is not a Part X Australian resident and is treated as a resident of that country for its tax law purposes (s 332). A company is resident in an unlisted country if it is not a Part X Australian resident and meets the tests in s 333 (treated as resident under the country's tax law, or if not, management-and-control or incorporation tests). A company resident only in Australia (a Part X Australian resident) is outside the CFC rules entirely.

nodes.label: Is the company a CFC — controlled by a small group of Australian entities?
nodes.body: A company is a CFC if it is a resident of a listed or unlisted country and any of these applies (s 340): (a) a group of 5 or fewer Australian 1% entities holds aggregate associate-inclusive control interests of at least 50%; (b) a single Australian entity holds at least 40% and no other group (not including that entity or its associates) controls the company; or (c) the company is actually controlled (de facto) by a group of 5 or fewer Australian entities, alone or with associates. Associate-inclusive control interest (s 349) aggregates direct and indirect control interests plus those of associates. The 1% rule in s 349(4) avoids double-counting where entities would each hold 100% through a chain.

nodes.label: Are you an attributable taxpayer — an Australian entity with a 10%+ associate-inclusive control interest?
nodes.body: An entity is an attributable taxpayer in relation to a CFC if it is an Australian entity whose associate-inclusive control interest in the CFC is at least 10% (s 361(1)(a)). Where the CFC is a CFC only because of the de facto control test (s 340(c)), an Australian 1% entity in the controlling group of 5 or fewer is also an attributable taxpayer (s 361(1)(b)). For a CFT the same 10% test applies (s 361(2)). Section 768-960 of the ITAA 1997 can override this — if a foreign resident is treated as an Australian resident under a DTA tie-breaker, the Commissioner may determine the entity is not an attributable taxpayer (interaction provision).

statute.title: Attributable taxpayer in relation to a CFC or a CFT
Commissioner may determine entity not attributable taxpayer

nodes.label: Work out your attribution percentage of the CFC
nodes.body: Your attribution percentage (s 362) is the percentage of the CFC's income attributed to you, worked out from your attribution tracing interests (ss 358-360) through direct and indirect holdings, including interposed entities. It is generally the proportion of the CFC you effectively own, directly and indirectly.

nodes.label: Does the CFC pass the active income test — tainted income ratio below 5%?
nodes.body:
The CFC passes the active income test (s 432) if, for the statutory accounting period: it was in existence at period end (s 432(1)(a)); it had no gap in foreign residency — meaning at every moment it existed it was a resident of a listed or unlisted country (s 432(1)(b), known as the foreign-residency continuity limb — this is NOT an Australian-residency test; Australian residency is the threshold question owned by the Part X Australian resident definition); it kept accounts to accepted principles giving a true and fair view (s 432(1)(c)); it complied with the substantiation requirements (s 451); it carried on business at or through a PE in its country of residence (s 432(1)(e)); and its tainted income ratio is less than 0.05 (s 432(1)(f), per s 433). Tainted income comprises passive income (s 446 — dividends, interest, annuities, rents, royalties, IP assignment proceeds, tainted asset trading, tainted commodity and currency gains), tainted sales income (s 447) and tainted services income (s 448).

Trading stock nuance: an asset held as trading stock is not a tainted asset (s 317(c)(i) carve-out), so turnover from trading stock sales (e.g. crypto traded as trading stock) stays in gross turnover but never reaches gross tainted turnover — it dilutes the ratio. The recognised accounts must actually classify it as trading stock revenue, or the s 434(1)(a)(ii) exclusion works against you.

nodes.label: Unlisted country CFC that fails the active income test: all income is attributed
nodes.body: For an unlisted country CFC that does not pass the active income test, s 384(2)(a) assumes the only notional assessable income is what would be included if all income derived were adjusted tainted income — effectively attributing the CFC's entire income (adjusted tainted income is defined in s 386 as passive, tainted sales and tainted services income with modifications). Amounts under the FIF rules (s 102AAZD) and Division 6 (trust) are also included (s 384(2)(b)-(c)).

statute.title: Additional assumption for unlisted country CFC
Adjusted tainted income

nodes.label: Unlisted country CFC that passes the active income test: only FIF and trust amounts are attributed
nodes.body: Where the CFC passes the active income test, s 384(2)(a) does not apply — only amounts under the FIF rules (s 102AAZD) and Division 6 (trust) are included in notional assessable income (s 384(2)(b)-(c)). The active business income is not attributed.

nodes.label: Listed country CFC that fails the active income test: only concession-income tainted amounts are attributed
nodes.body: For a listed country CFC that does not pass the active income test, s 385(2)(a) assumes the only notional assessable income is: adjusted tainted income that is eligible designated concession income in relation to the listed country (or another listed country), plus regulation-specified amounts that are not eligible designated concession income, are not treated as derived from sources in the listed country, and pass the test in s 385(2A). FIF (s 102AAZD) and Division 6 amounts are also included (s 385(2)(b)-(c)).

statute.title: Additional assumption for listed country CFC

nodes.label: Listed country CFC that passes the active income test: only regulation, FIF and trust amounts are attributed
nodes.body: Where the CFC passes the active income test, s 385(2)(a) does not apply — only the regulation-specified amounts, FIF (s 102AAZD) and Division 6 (trust) amounts are included in notional assessable income (s 385(2)(b)-(d)).

nodes.label: Calculate the attributable income — taxable income on modified assumptions
nodes.body: Attributable income is the amount that would be the CFC's taxable income for the period if the assumptions in s 382-383 were made: the CFC is a taxpayer and resident; the period is a year of income; the Act is modified in accordance with Subdivisions B-E of Division 7; and the s 384 or 385 assumption applies. Key modifications: notional assessable amounts are taken pre-tax (s 392); a notional deduction is allowed for foreign taxes paid (s 393); double tax agreements are disregarded (s 388); certain provisions are disregarded (ss 389, 389A); and attributable income is reduced by interim dividends (s 387).

nodes.label: Your attribution percentage of the attributable income is included in your assessable income
nodes.body: Under s 456, your attribution percentage of the CFC's attributable income is included in your assessable income for the year of income in which the statutory accounting period ends. Where the item has already been subject to foreign accruals tax in a listed country at its normal company tax rate, the amount is reduced under s 456A. If the CFC changed residence (e.g. unlisted to listed) during the period, s 457 limits attribution to the parts of the period in which it was resident in the relevant country.

nodes.label: Track the attribution accounts — surplus = attribution credits minus debits
nodes.body: The attribution account system (Division 4) prevents double taxation of attributed income when it is later distributed. An attribution account entity is a company that is not a Part X Australian resident, a partnership or a trust (s 363). An attribution surplus exists when total attribution credits exceed total attribution debits (s 370). Credits arise when income is attributed (s 371); debits arise on distributions to you (s 372).

Attribution credit

nodes.label: Distributions of attributed income are non-assessable — the attribution surplus is debited
nodes.body: When the CFC distributes profits that have already been attributed to you, the distribution is not taxed again: an attribution debit arises (s 372), reducing the attribution surplus. This is the mechanism that makes attributed income effectively taxed on an accrual basis, with distributions flowing out tax-free to the extent of the surplus.

nodes.label: Disposing of your interest: capital proceeds are reduced by the attribution surplus
nodes.body: If you dispose of an interest in an attribution account entity (or a CGT event happens) while an attribution surplus exists, the consideration or capital proceeds are reduced by the surplus (s 461), so you are not taxed again on income already attributed. An attribution debit arises at the time of the disposal (s 372), with no grossed-up amount (s 373).

statute.title: Reduction of disposal consideration or capital proceeds if attributed income not distributed

nodes.label: Keep records of the CFC and its attributable income
nodes.body: Division 11 requires attributable taxpayers to keep records sufficient to work out their liability (s 462), in writing in English or readily accessible and convertible into English, kept so the liability can be readily ascertained (s 466). Failure to keep records is an offence (s 465).

nodes.label: No attribution — the CFC's income is not included in your assessable income
nodes.body: Where the company is not a CFC, you are not an attributable taxpayer, or the CFC passes the active income test (with only limited amounts attributed), the company's income is not attributed to you. It may be taxed later as a dividend when distributed, and other regimes (transfer pricing, the anti-avoidance rules, the CGT rules for foreign interests) may still apply.

nodes.label: Attribution applies — income taxed now, distributions tax-free later
nodes.body: Your attribution percentage of the CFC's attributable income is taxed in the year the statutory accounting period ends. The attribution account system then lets the income flow out as tax-free distributions (or a reduced capital gain on disposal), keeping the total tax at the attribution stage.

nodes.label: Is, or has the company become, a Part X Australian resident?
nodes.body: A company that is a Part X Australian resident (resident in Australia under section 6 of the ITAA 1936, subject to tie-breaker rules in double tax agreements) cannot be a CFC. Section 340 defines a CFC as a company resident in a listed or unlisted country. Sections 332(2)(a) and 333(2)(a) each require that the company NOT be a Part X Australian resident. If the company IS a Part X Australian resident, the whole CFC analysis is displaced — it falls outside Part X entirely. A company that becomes a Part X Australian resident mid-period triggers the residence-change rules (s 457), which may tax accumulated undistributed tainted income.
